default.reply: Thank you for sharing this with me 💙 It matters to me to understand you better. Would you like to share a bit more about what's on your mind the most — studies, sleep, relationships, or how you're feeling lately? Whatever you say, I'm here for you patiently.

ai.disclaimer: The responses in this conversation are written by AI, not a human; this is an educational companion and is not a substitute for professional counseling. In critical situations, call the helpline {phone}.

greeting.high: Hello 😄 It's great that you're feeling good today! Let's use this energy to build a productive day. What's on your mind?
greeting.low: Hello 💙 I see you're not feeling your best today. I'm glad you're here — just wanting to talk is a kind step toward yourself. Write to me whatever you'd like, I'm listening patiently.
greeting.mid: Hello 🌤️ I am your AI psychology companion. Write whatever is on your mind — studies, stress, sleep, or even a good mood — so we can look at it together.
greeting.none: Hello 🙂 I am your AI psychology companion; a safe and confidential space to talk. How are your days going lately? We can talk about anything you'd like.

gratitude.reply1: You're very welcome 💙 I'm so glad I could be here for you. Remember that this progress is the result of your own effort and openness. Whenever you need help again, I'm right here.
gratitude.tip1: Record this good mood with a short note for yourself
gratitude.tip2: Do a kind act for yourself or someone else

happy.reply1: Wow, that's wonderful! 🎉 I'm so glad you're feeling well — this positive energy is worth celebrating. Let's make sure this good feeling lasts and use it to help you reach your goals.
happy.reply2: This news warmed my heart too! 🌟 Mindfully savor these good moments; they are what give us strength on difficult days. Be proud of yourself.
happy.tip1: Note down this good moment so you can return to it later
happy.tip2: Focusing on this energy, take one small step toward your goal
happy.tip3: Share your good mood with someone you love

lonely.reply1: Missing home and feeling lonely, especially far from home, is one of the hardest parts of student life, and you're not alone in it 💙 This feeling means you have valuable connections. Let's find ways to both stay in touch with your loved ones and build a sense of belonging here.
lonely.tip1: Schedule a short, regular call with your family
lonely.tip2: Join a student club or group that shares your interests
lonely.tip3: Start a small conversation with a classmate today

motivation.reply1: A drop in motivation happens to all of us and it's not a sign of laziness on your part — it's often a sign of fatigue or goals that are too big. Let's make the goal small enough so that it's easy to start; movement builds motivation, not the other way around. 🌱
motivation.reply2: When motivation dips, instead of waiting for the 'right feeling', just start for two minutes. Often those two minutes get the wheels turning. Be proud of yourself for still being here and trying.
motivation.tip1: Focus only on the 'first two-minute step', not the whole task
motivation.tip2: Set a small reward for the end of each study session
motivation.tip3: See your progress: write down one tiny thing you accomplished today

sad.reply1: I'm sorry you're feeling a heaviness on your heart these days 💙 Your feelings are completely valid and you don't need to hide them. The fact that you're talking about it is a sign of your strength, not your weakness. Let's take it step by step.
sad.reply2: I want you to know that you're not alone in this feeling and this state will pass, even if it doesn't seem like it right now. Be kinder to yourself than ever; you deserve that kindness.
sad.tip1: Do a small, pleasant thing for yourself (music, short walk, tea)
sad.tip2: Write down three things you feel grateful for today
sad.tip3: Reach out to a friend or a trusted person; being seen helps

sleep.reply1: Good sleep is the foundation of everything — both peace of mind and focus in studies. If your sleep has been disrupted these past nights, it's totally normal; a busy mind has a hard time settling down. Let's review a few simple habits together to bring back your sleep quality.
sleep.tip1: Put screens away an hour before bedtime
sleep.tip2: Keep the room cool and dark and go to sleep at the same time every night
sleep.tip3: If you can't fall asleep for 20 minutes, get up and do a relaxing activity

stress.reply1: I completely understand; exam stress and study pressure are really heavy and this feeling is completely natural. Your body is trying to get ready, just a little too much. Let's bring calmness back to your mind together — you've got this.
stress.reply2: I sense that you're under pressure and that's hard. It's important to know that anxiety means you care about this matter, not that you're incapable. Take a deep breath; I'm right here with you.
stress.tip1: 4-7-8 breathing exercise: four seconds inhale, seven seconds hold, eight seconds exhale
stress.tip2: Break tasks down into small 25-minute steps (Pomodoro)
stress.tip3: Drink a glass of water and step away from your desk for two minutes

study.reply1: When study planning is set up right, it removes a large part of the stress on its own. Focus is a skill, not a fixed trait — it gets stronger with practice. Let's create a simple and workable rhythm for you so you can make progress without getting exhausted.
study.tip1: Work using the Pomodoro technique: 25 minutes of focus + 5 minutes of rest
study.tip2: Put your mobile phone on Do Not Disturb and out of reach
study.tip3: Read the hardest subject first thing in the morning, when you have more energy
